title: A 1.7% inflation print was consistent with an unchanged ECB outlook
summary: January inflation was 1.7%, yet Christine Lagarde described the Council’s 5 February decision to leave rates unchanged as unanimous. The main question at the press conference was what a below-target print revealed about the medium-term outlook. Energy was pulling the aggregate down while services inflation remained above 3%. A stronger euro was already reflected in the baseline, and fourth-quarter investment was supporting activity even as net exports struggled. These were different signals about future prices. Lagarde declined to turn their combination into an unconditional promise to ease or tighten.

The composition of the inflation decline made her reasoning concrete. Headline inflation had been 2.1% in November and 2.0% in December. January energy inflation was −4.1% in the prepared statement, compared with −1.9% in December, while food inflation rose from 2.5% to 2.7%. Goods inflation edged up to 0.4%. Services inflation fell from 3.4% to 3.2%, and the measure excluding energy and food fell from 2.3% to 2.2%. Lagarde stressed energy base effects in her answers. She also saw the easing in services as consistent with the anticipated adjustment toward the target. A weaker headline print and progress on domestic inflation were both present, but neither implied that the projection had shifted materially. The ECB still saw inflation at 2% in 2028.

The wage evidence supported patience with a specific qualification. Negotiated wages and the ECB’s forward-looking wage indicators suggested moderation. Payments beyond negotiated rates, including wage drift and one-offs, were harder to pin down. Labour demand had cooled and vacancies were increasing more slowly, yet participation had increased and unemployment fell from 6.3% to 6.2% in December. Lagarde pointed out that labour indicators arriving in January could refer back to the third or fourth quarter. A convincing assessment of services costs therefore required matching pay, employment and vacancies by the period they described. The latest publication date alone would yield a misleading chronology.

Output had grown 0.3% in the fourth quarter on the preliminary flash estimate available at the meeting. Information and communication services helped drive growth. Construction was gaining momentum with support from public investment. Private investment included software, hardware and the infrastructure needed for data centres, with some projects still in the authorisation process. Lagarde distinguished evidence of investment spending from the productivity gains that might eventually follow it. The former could lift demand now. The latter would depend on how effectively the investment was used and might take longer to affect unit costs. Consumption was improving more slowly, while tariffs and the stronger euro complicated the outlook for exporters.

The exchange-rate discussion also turned on the timing of the news. Lagarde placed the material dollar depreciation against the euro back in March 2025 and described trading since the summer as a range, both bilaterally and in the nominal effective measure. The previous appreciation had already been built into the ECB baseline. A researcher looking for fresh downside risk to inflation would need evidence of additional appreciation or unexpectedly strong pass-through. The Council described risks overall as broadly balanced in discussion, with a wide range of possible outcomes. It did not adopt an exchange-rate target. Separately, Lagarde described work to make repo lines more accessible to foreign central banks. That concerned the provision of euro liquidity and carried no quantitative exchange-rate objective.

Transmission was uneven across markets and borrowers. Market rates had fallen since the previous meeting, but the rate on new corporate bank loans rose from 3.5% in November to 3.6% in December. The new mortgage rate held at 3.3%. The bank lending survey showed slightly stronger corporate loan demand for working capital and inventories alongside another tightening of corporate credit standards. Mortgage credit standards eased and demand continued to rise. Corporate loan and mortgage lending balances each grew 3.0% year on year in December, despite these different conditions for new borrowers. The relevant signal for demand was therefore less uniform than either a common ECB rate or identical annual loan growth rates might suggest. The press conference reports developments between meetings and earlier monthly loan observations. Neither is a measured market reaction to the 5 February decision.

questions.question: Was the disinflation in services broad enough to persist?
questions.detail: Compare sector-level services inflation with negotiated wage increases, employers’ actual compensation payments and productivity. Align the reference periods and identify one-offs. The wedge between negotiated and actual labour costs matters for whether the observed moderation in services can continue after favourable energy base effects fade.

questions.question: Which borrowers received relief from lower market rates?
questions.detail: Trace corporate new-loan rates and mortgage pricing alongside standards, demand and volumes. Distinguish working-capital credit from financing for new fixed investment. The survey pointed to different conditions for businesses and households, so a common change in short-term market rates is unlikely to explain both groups equally well.

questions.question: Did the euro produce more disinflation than the baseline allowed?
questions.detail: Recover the exchange-rate path embodied in the forecast and compare it with both the realised effective rate and import prices. Where possible distinguish price changes in foreign currency from exchange-rate pass-through. Evidence of weaker pricing by exporters to the euro area could change the interpretation even if the bilateral exchange rate stayed in its range.

questions.question: Did investment in technology already raise output per hour?
questions.detail: Follow the progression from licensing and capital expenditure to completed facilities, software adoption and measured productivity. This separates immediate demand associated with construction and procurement from later supply effects. It also bears on how much of the domestic investment strength could offset weakness in net exports.
